title: concurrent-kv-lock-heap-pressure-retro-and-runbook-wip
body:
Summary:

Short version: a regression in the continuous batching / prefetch path caused unusually long-held KV-cache locks under high concurrency which amplified heap pressure and produced OOM-like symptoms on a subset of hosts. The incident surface was intermittent request stalls, degraded tail latency, and several host reboots from OOM kill. This doc captures the triage timeline, temporary containment steps used by on-call, a short runbook for similar events, and proposed follow-ups (code + monitoring).

Impact:
- Time window: 2024-11-10 03:12 - 2024-11-10 06:04 UTC (active anomalies)
- Affected fleet: serving-runtime gpu-pool-3, ~22% of hosts experienced elevated memory usage, 6 hosts OOM-killed and drained.
- Customer-visible: intermittent 500s and streaming stalls for hosted customers on models >8k context when traffic spiked. No data loss.

Detection and signals:
- First pager triggered by tail-latency SLO alert for route /v1/generate (alert: tail_p99_latency > 1200ms sustained).
- SRE dashboards showed rising kvcache.lock_hold_ms (metric added earlier this year) and a growing queue of blocking batch workers (batch.queue_stalled_count).
- Hosts with issues showed: sustained high RSS, kswapd activity, and LRU eviction spikes for process serving-runtime.
- On some hosts kernel OOM killer logs referencing the serving-runtime process.

Initial hypothesis (fast):
- Regression in prefetch/continuous-batching introduced a code path that can acquire the global KV-cache lock while doing blocking I/O or memory allocations. Under concurrent requests the lock hold time balloons, preventing other requests from progressing and causing memory usage to accumulate (no KV eviction until lock released). This produces a feedback loop: blocked batches queue up, memory growth continues, and OOM ensues.

Investigation timeline (high level):
- 03:15 UTC: Pager -> SRE takes ownership, posts to #sre-oncall
- 03:22 UTC: Observed kvcache.lock_hold_ms correlated with latency; concurrent batch workers > 40 on affected hosts
- 03:30 UTC: Narrowed to gpu-pool-3; reproduced locally by replaying traffic; saw single thread holding kv lock for tens of seconds
- 04:05 UTC: Deployed temporary containment: reduce continuous-batching max concurrency on pool (config flag: serving.batch.max_concurrency=8) and disable aggressive prefetch (serving.kv.prefetch=false)
- 04:18 UTC: Metrics improved; lock_hold_ms returned to baseline; heap growth slowed; no further OOM kills after hosts drained/restarted
- 05:20 UTC: Rollback of the suspect PR (was part of PR #4892) to remove new blocking code path
- 06:04 UTC: Incident declared mitigated; monitoring remained stable

Short-term containment used by oncall (playbook steps executed):
1) Route-level throttling: quickly reduce concurrency for heavy context routes via traffic-router feature flags (route: /v1/generate-bigctx -> qps cap 50%)
2) Adjust runtime config for affected pool:
   - serving.batch.max_concurrency: drop from 32 -> 8
   - serving.kv.prefetch: false (disable prefetch path)
3) Drain and reboot hosts with persistent high RSS (automated hosts were drained via sdb-drain-host)
4) If OOMs continue: scale up replacement hosts in pool while draining failing hosts

Oncall runbook (concise checklist for next time):
- Trigger: tail latency > SLO OR host OOM kill with process name serving-runtime
- Quick triage commands:
  - kubectl -n serving get pods -l pool=gpu-pool-3 -o wide
  - ssh <host> dmesg | grep -i oom
  - curl -s http://localhost:7070/metrics | grep kvcache.lock_hold_ms
  - curl -s http://localhost:7070/metrics | grep batch.queue_stalled_count
  - ps aux --sort=-rss | head -n 10
- Immediate mitigations:
  - Toggle serving.kv.prefetch=false via featureconfig for the pool
  - Reduce serving.batch.max_concurrency
  - If lock_hold_ms > 2000ms: set route throttle at 50% for affected routes
- Communication: post status in #sre-oncall and tag product-owner and infra on Slack; update incident doc with timeline and commands executed

Root cause (detailed):
- The change introduced in PR #4892 added a synchronous cold-fetch path in the KV prefetching logic that allocates large scratch buffers while holding the central kvcache mutex. Previously the mutex protected only short indexing work. Under contention the thread holding the mutex could end up blocked in allocation/IO and not release the mutex. This prevented concurrent threads from servicing their requests or evicting cached items, causing heap to grow unbounded for live requests.
- Secondary contributor: continuous batching increases burst concurrency; some host capacity assumptions (memory headroom per batch worker) were optimistic and did not account for long lock hold scenarios.

Immediate code-level fixes proposed (short-medium term):
- Short: revert the blocking cold-fetch path (done during incident) and re-introduce instrumentation around any code that acquires the global lock
- Medium: refactor kvcache to use per-shard locks (shard by key-hash) so that a single slow key does not stall whole host
- Medium: convert cold-fetch to a try-lock + background fetch with a callback that inserts into cache asynchronously (avoid holding lock across allocation or blocking IO)
- Long: add admission control to continuous batching to enforce memory headroom limits per host and graceful backpressure when memory budget is low

Monitoring and alerting follow-ups (to create):
- New alerts:
  - kvcache.lock_hold_ms > 500ms sustained 1m -> warn; >2000ms -> page SRE
  - batch.queue_stalled_count > 10 for more than 2m -> page SRE
  - host.rss_high_count > 5 (per node) -> page SRE
- Dashboards:
  - Per-pool lock hold time heatmap
  - Correlation panel: lock_hold_ms vs host.rss vs eviction_rate
- Synthetic tests: add a chaos test that simulates a slow cold-fetch path and validates per-shard lock fallback (once implemented)

Open questions and TODOs:
- How often is our kvcache cold fetch actually hitting remote storage under real traffic? (need sampling data)
- Should we instrument worst-case allocation size inside lock to quantify risk? (PR to add allocation-size histograms)
- Where else do we hold global locks during allocations? run a code grep for "Mutex" + large alloc in serving-runtime repo
- Consider memory-aware scheduling on hosts (reject new batches if per-host mem budget > 85%)

Post-incident action items (owner, ETA):
- Fix: refactor cold-fetch (owner: Ethan Liu) - ETA 2025-01-15 (RFC + incremental PRs)
- Monitoring: add lock_hold_ms paging thresholds and dashboard (owner: Priya Rao) - ETA 2024-12-10
- Load test: create synthetic for slow-cold-fetch with high concurrency (owner: Noah Patel) - ETA 2024-12-03
- Runbook: formalize the above checklist into Playbooks repo and link oncall runbooks (owner: Aisha Khan) - ETA 2024-11-30

Notes-to-self / observed oddities:
- Not all hosts in pool were affected; pattern suggests hosts with slightly older kernel or different NUMA layout reached OOM faster (need host-metadata sweep)
- Reproduced locally only when replaying realistic batch interleaving; unit tests didn't catch because they simulated single-threaded behavior

Appendix: useful logs and snippets (paste key snippets here in incident doc)
- dmesg sample: "[12345.678901] Out of memory: Killed process 4321 (serving-runtime) total-vm:12345678kB"
- metrics snapshot: kvcache.lock_hold_ms  "p50: 12ms p90: 350ms p99: 2200ms"

End of draft.

If you are reviewing: add any missing context, correct ETA assignments, and flag any follow-ups that should be higher priority. We should schedule a postmortem review with serving-runtime owners next week.
